Women need equal access to the opportunities.","heroVisual":{"alt":"Illustration of women working across generations of computing, from handwritten calculations and punch cards to modern AI.","credit":"LAiDIES","src":"/assets/newsstand/design-20260830/front-paige-women-computing.png"},"id":"front-paige-accountable-systems-2026-08-24","laidies_read":"

Our concern is how employers distribute the opportunities that come with AI: a place on a project, time to learn, a leadership role or a say in how a job changes. Telling women to practise more does not answer who gets those opportunities.

Imagine two equally interested colleagues. One is given an approved AI tool, paid time to try it and an invitation to help evaluate a new process. The other is told to keep up, without those arrangements. If the first colleague uses AI more often, that alone would tell us little about the second colleague’s enthusiasm or ability. This is an example of why conditions matter, not a finding about what caused the survey gap.

The next decision matters too. If a manager selects a team to test a new AI tool only from people already using it, someone who never had supported access can miss another opportunity. Employers can examine how they choose participants, provide learning time and recognize the work of testing and checking AI. More logins, by themselves, would not tell us whether those decisions had become fairer.

Women accounted for 26% of U.S. hires into AI occupations in 2025, compared with 50% of hires into other occupations, according to research LinkedIn published on August 18. Its separate international leadership analysis found that women held 13% of top executive AI leadership roles at AI companies. These figures describe who is getting hired and who holds authority.

A U.S. Census Bureau report published on August 11 measures something different: how often people use AI at work. Among workers who had used AI for at least one of the tasks surveyed, 30% of men and 17% of women reported using it every day in the previous week. The survey was conducted in March 2026.

Those are different groups and different questions. The hiring figures do not cover every job in which someone uses AI. The frequency figures do not measure skill, interest or whether daily use would help someone do her job. Neither report establishes why a particular woman has less access to an opportunity.

If there’s an opportunity to learn about AI or help decide how it’s used at work, you can ask to take part. Ask questions when something doesn’t make sense—even if you think everyone else already knows the answer. You don’t need to arrive as an expert to contribute.

Employers should make those opportunities visible, provide time and support to learn, and welcome questions rather than assume everyone starts with the same knowledge.

Among workers who had used AI for at least one of the tasks surveyed, 30% of men and 17% of women reported using it every day in the previous week. The survey was conducted in March 2026. [P004] Those are different groups and different questions. The hiring figures do not cover every job in which someone uses AI. The frequency figures do not measure skill, interest or whether daily use would help someone do her job. Neither report establishes why a particular woman has less access to an opportunity. [P005] Our concern is how employers distribute the opportunities that come with AI: a place on a project, time to learn, a leadership role or a say in how a job changes. Telling women to practise more does not answer who gets those opportunities. [P006] Imagine two equally interested colleagues. One is given an approved AI tool, paid time to try it and an invitation to help evaluate a new process. The other is told to keep up, without those arrangements. If the first colleague uses AI more often, that alone would tell us little about the second colleague’s enthusiasm or ability. This is an example of why conditions matter, not a finding about what caused the survey gap. [P007] The next decision matters too. If a manager selects a team to test a new AI tool only from people already using it, someone who never had supported access can miss another opportunity. Employers can examine how they choose participants, provide learning time and recognize the work of testing and checking AI. More logins, by themselves, would not tell us whether those decisions had become fairer. [P008] If there’s an opportunity to learn about AI or help decide how it’s used at work, you can ask to take part. Ask questions when something doesn’t make sense—even if you think everyone else already knows the answer. You don’t need to arrive as an expert to contribute. [P009] Employers should make those opportunities visible, provide time and support to learn, and welcome questions rather than assume everyone starts with the same knowledge. [P010] “These reports show gaps in AI hiring, leadership and daily workplace use. They do not show that women lack interest or ability. Employers need to examine who gets the tools, learning time and opportunities to take part.” [P011] When you encounter a statistic about AI use, ask who was measured, what was measured and whether the research explains why. A difference in frequency is not a measure of ability. RUBRIC AND EVIDENCE: {"communicationAuthority":{"sha256":"7d61a0e17d5ad6809d1d1e6931d297b42e443a3027a97fb7c16432f3f8aecff3","text":"# Hannah Fry communication benchmark **Status:** ACTIVE INTERNAL EXPLANATION LENS **Benchmark ID:** `HANNAH_FRY_COMMUNICATION_LENS_V2` **Owner:** Learning System & Concepts Director ## Purpose and boundary This benchmark adapts communication mechanics previously analysed from Hannah Fry's public science communication. It is not permission to imitate her voice, persona, mannerisms, identity or the structure of a particular talk or book. Her name is not evidence that a draft is clear or engaging. The LAiDIES producer must translate the useful mechanics into the cognitive job and scale of the destination. A class can support prediction, demonstration and transfer. A book can create curiosity, make a hidden process concrete and route a better next question without becoming a lecture. A reference, FAQ, practice item, interactive or NewsStand explanation uses only the moves that improve its own job. Promotional copy and microcopy declare the lens not applicable rather than manufacturing teaching. ## Communication dimensions 1. **Human question:** begin from a reason the learner already has to care, choose, notice or challenge—not from terminology for its own sake. 2. **Useful curiosity:** invite a prediction, tension, surprise or question only when the answer will reveal the mechanism. A hook without explanatory payoff fails. 3. **Invisible process made concrete:** use the smallest faithful case, demonstration, diagram, comparison or sequence that lets the learner see what otherwise happens out of view. 4. **Familiar and technical movement:** connect ordinary experience to the correct abstraction and then return to the real system. A familiar example that never reconnects to the mechanism is decoration. 5. **Limitations and consequences:** retain where the explanation stops, what can go wrong, uncertainty, misuse and why the distinction matters. 6. **Humour and surprise:** use them only when they sharpen attention, distinction or recall without making the learner or subject childish. `NOT_APPLICABLE` is often the right choice. 7. **Better next question:** leave the learner able to ask, test or notice something more precise than before. ## Default substantial-explanation arc Ali's supplied [analysis reel](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DazjzEQo4gP/) adds an ordering rule to the dimensions above. The direct Instagram fetch was throttled during the 2026-08-08 evidence check; a public [cross-platform transcript](https://tokscribe.com/t/cmrm19jj202oi140r806a97qv) records the creator's observational analysis of 30 high-performing Hannah Fry videos. Treat that analysis as a communication-pattern source, not an experimental proof of learning effectiveness. For an episode, class or substantial explanation, the default arc is: 1. **Shared starting point and live question:** begin with a physical, everyday or work experience the learner can picture, then open a precise gap she has a reason to resolve. 2. **Mechanism, link by link:** spend the centre and largest share of the explanation on cause and effect. Let the learner follow the discovery; do not substitute suspense, analogy or personality for the mechanism. 3. **Earned click:** after the mechanism, resolve the gap with the distinction, correction or consequence that makes her think “oh, I get it now.” Do not hide a direct safety-critical answer merely to manufacture a reveal. 4. **Small landing:** finish with a precise observation, useful action, better question or earned joke. Do not inflate a bounded explanation into a grand inspirational moral. This is a default explanatory sequence, not a sentence template. An FAQ, reference, breaking-news item or safety instruction may need the direct answer first; it records a proportional adaptation rather than distorting its real job to imitate a reel. ## Generation rule Before drafting, the producer records which dimensions apply, why, the exact experience or prose move planned for each, the destination-specific adaptation and the no-imitation boundary. Full explanations apply at least six dimensions and bind the four-part arc's shared starting point, curiosity gap, causal sequence, earned click and small landing. Proportional formats apply at least two dimensions and either adapt named arc moves or explain why the sequence would obstruct their job. The record fails if it merely says "Hannah Fry inspired." ## Review and learning-loop rule The producer and independent reviewer inspect the exact artifact for evidence that the applied moves improve understanding and engagement while preserving technical truth. For a full explanation, they also locate the actual starting point, causal sequence, earned click and landing in the artifact. They reject name-dropping, curiosity without payoff, a familiar example with no technical return, pastiche, a reveal before the mechanism earns it, a hook that receives more attention than the explanation, entertainment before understanding and an inflated ending. Any newly observed reusable failure follows the shared learning-disposition route; feedback cannot automatically rewrite, retire or unpublish content. ## Existing basis Version 1 consolidated the already adopted analysis in `operations/classes/CLASS-MEDIA-PRODUCTION-STANDARD.md` and `operations/product-stewards/LEARNING-CONTENT-STANDARD.md`. The research basis and its 2026-08-02 check date remain in the Classes standard. Version 2 adds Ali's 2026-08-08 ordering decision from the supplied reel analysis. Because producer contracts bind the exact benchmark bytes, this revision invalidates stale communication designs before further drafting. A future evidence refresh may revise this lens through Learning-owner admission; it may not silently change an in-flight producer contract.
